explanations.explanation: Right on the money, friend. The psalm says it plain: "In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me." (Psalm 120:1) The writer cried out and the LORD answered. That's the whole opening, and everything after it gets told from that spot.
Close, but the text says the opposite, friend. Psalm 120:1 says, "In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me." So the writer did cry out, and the LORD did answer.

explanations.answer: Lying lips and a deceitful tongue
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! That's exactly what the writer asks to be delivered from: "…lying lips and a deceitful tongue." (Psalm 120:2) Notice what the trouble is. It isn't swords or soldiers, it's words that aren't true. I think words like that can sting plenty.

explanations.answer: A strong enemy and a mighty army
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since an army sounds like big trouble. But the prayer names something different. The writer asks to be delivered from "…lying lips and a deceitful tongue." (Psalm 120:2) No army is mentioned in this prayer, just words that can't be trusted.

explanations.answer: Hunger and a dry and weary land
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend. A dry and weary land sounds like a rough place to be. But the writer prays to be delivered from "…lying lips and a deceitful tongue." (Psalm 120:2) Hunger and dry land never show up in this psalm.

That's it, baker! "Sharp arrows will come from the warrior…" (Psalm 120:4) The song asks the deceitful tongue what will be done to it, and the warrior's arrows show up right after. Whoa. Nobody wants that kind of delivery.

A warrior with a shield makes sense, friend. But that's not what the verse gives us. It says, "Sharp arrows will come from the warrior, with burning coals of the broom tree!" (Psalm 120:4) What comes from him is arrows, not something to hide behind.

Sounds like a warrior outfit, I'll give you that. But the verse says what comes from the warrior is "Sharp arrows," with burning coals of the broom tree. (Psalm 120:4) No helmet in sight. Honestly, I'd be wearing my chef's hat and praying.

Not quite, friend. The writer says, "Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar!" (Psalm 120:5) "Woe to me…" is not what a happy person says. I think the writer is hurting over living there.

Right, baker! The writer cries, "Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar!" (Psalm 120:5) Nobody says "Woe to me…" while smiling. Meshech and Kedar are home, but this is no happy home.
You got it, baker. The writer says, "Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace." (Psalm 120:6) So it's not only the place, it's the people around the writer. That would wear anybody down.
Not this time, friend. The verse says the writer lives among "…those who hate peace." (Psalm 120:6) Keeping peace would make for a calmer neighbor. These people are the opposite of that.
I get it, "seek peace" sounds like a nice phrase. But the writer says "Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace." (Psalm 120:6) These neighbors aren't looking for peace at all. They hate it.
Other way around, friend. The writer says, "Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace." (Psalm 120:6) The writer calls it too long, not a short while. I think the writer is worn out.
Yes, baker! The writer says, "Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace." (Psalm 120:6) Too long is the writer's own word for it. It isn't described as a short while.

Right, baker. "I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war." (Psalm 120:7) The writer is in favor of peace. But when the writer speaks, they want war. I think that's a hard spot to be in, and I bet it wears a person out.

Quiet sounds like a decent guess, friend. But the verse says, "I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war." (Psalm 120:7) The writer is in favor of peace, and when the writer speaks, they want war.

Trade is a fun guess, but not what the verse says. It reads, "I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war." (Psalm 120:7) The writer is in favor of peace, and when the writer speaks, they want war.
